**Audience**: an engineer with a RAG / fine-tune notebook who must ship it. **Empirical first**: p95 latency 4.2 s because the retriever is not batched; cost ×3 after an unversioned prompt change; then we name tracing, eval harness, guardrails.

From notebook to system: version, serve, monitor and cost-control LLM apps.

### What you will be able to do

-   Version data, features, and models with usable lineage (reproduce an experiment from six months ago);
-   Build a CI/CD pipeline that tests data and models, not just code;
-   Serve an LLM with continuous batching and reason in P99 latency rather than averages;
-   Quantify the cost of an application in euros per million tokens and arbitrate between APIs, fine-tuning, and distillation;
-   Detect and handle drift (data, predictions) with monitoring that alerts when appropriate;
-   Operate a RAG system: index freshness, continuous evaluation, unanswered queries;
-   Deploy versioned LoRA fine-tunings and traced agents with their guardrails;
-   Secure the whole: secrets, sandbox, supply chain, and master the carbon footprint of your services.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module offered in period 2, outside the recommended track: it is the master's "systems" course, designed for profiles aiming at engineering as much as research. **Prerequisites**: [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) provides the architecture and inference foundations instrumented here, and [Deep Learning (P2 variant)](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html) raised the training-cost and serving questions now handled in production.

**Downstream**: this module directly arms the master's cross-cutting project and the end-of-studies internship — ML/LLM engineer job interviews probe almost word for word its chapters (latency, costs, drift, RAG, agents). It also gives research profiles the vocabulary and constraints for their prototypes to become deployable.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: from notebook to system** — why scaling up breaks the implicit assumptions of notebook work.
-   **Lifecycle: versioning data, features, models** — lineage, reproducibility, and long-term artifact management.
-   **CI/CD for ML: testing data and models** — extending continuous integration to datasets and model metrics.
-   **LLM serving: continuous batching, P99 latency** — what happens between the prompt and the first token, and how to control it.
-   **Costs: euros per million tokens** — modeling the total cost of a service and steering it.
-   **Evaluation in production: drift and monitoring** — detecting that the world has changed under the model's feet.
-   **RAG Ops: freshness and continuous evaluation** — operating a living index and measuring answer quality over time.
-   **Fine-tuning Ops: versioned LoRAs** — lightweight trainings, adapters managed like code, possible rollback.
-   **Agents in production: tracing and guardrails** — trajectory observability, action limits, error budgets.
-   **Operational security: secrets, sandbox, supply chain** — protecting the accesses, execution, and dependencies of an ML system.
-   **Case study and green ops** — a complete architecture examined end to end, financial and carbon costs included.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — instrumenting a mini-system: versioning, CI, serving, drift monitoring.
-   **References** — documented tools and reference texts of ML Ops.

### How to study this module

-   Treat each chapter as a code review more than a course: what matters is the operational detail (alert thresholds, budgets, naming conventions), not the grand principles.
-   Instrument from the first lab onward: measuring the latency and cost of *your* API calls builds the intuition that reading alone does not give.
-   Keep a cost spreadsheet up to date throughout the module: it is the artifact that later serves in interviews and internships.
-   Read the public post-mortems and incident reports of ML systems cited by the module: the essentials of the trade are learned from others' failures.
-   Connect with [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) in every chapter: every ops decision (batching, quantization, caching) corresponds to an architecture mechanism you have already studied.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} The LLGA master trains profiles able to do research *and* to put it into production; this module is the pivot of that promise. LLMs are treated here as what they have become in companies: components of a system, with their latencies, their costs, and their failure modes — and the reflexes acquired here (measure, version, monitor) apply equally well to the graph models and tabular pipelines encountered in the other modules.
:::

## 0. Reminders: from notebook to system {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1/M2 modules)
:::

-   **LLMs** (LLMs M2 module): architecture and training (ch. 2-3), SFT/RLHF/DPO post-training (ch. 4-5), *inference and serving with vLLM* (ch. 6), RAG (ch. 7), agents (ch. 8), evaluation and safety (ch. 9) — this module extends ch. 6 into engineering;
-   **Deep Learning** (M1): PyTorch training loops, GPU, checkpoints — the foundation of what must be industrialized;
-   **ML** (M1): generalization theory, concentration (Hoeffding) — used in ch. 2 to bound non-regression tests;
-   **RL** (M1): bandits (ch. 6) for A/B tests and model routing;
-   **Refresher CS** (M1): containers, queues, complexity — the system vocabulary of serving (ch. 3).
::::

**The founding observation.** A model reaching 92% F1 in a notebook does not "work": it works *in an environment*. The founding paper of the field (Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015) shows that ML technical debt lives not in the model but around it: data pipelines, glue code, dependency chains, configurations, and *feedback loops* — the model in production influences the data that will be used to retrain it. The LLM does not abolish this debt; it adds three specificities: the model is *non-deterministic*, its *input space* is all of natural language (hence not boundable by a schema), and its *unit cost* (the token) is billed on every request.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — ML Ops]{.tag} The set of software, data, and systems engineering practices applied to the complete lifecycle of a machine learning system: development, testing, integration, deployment, monitoring, retraining. *LLM engineering* is the special case where the central component is a language model (API or open weights), typically within a RAG, a fine-tuning, or an agent.
:::

                        Classical software       Traditional ML           LLM application
  --------------------- ------------------------ ------------------------ ----------------------------------------------
  Unit of test          Function, API contract   Validation set, metric   Eval set + judge + prompt contracts
  Visible regression    Exception, crash         Metric drop              *Fuzzy* degradation: style, hallucinations
  Inputs                Typed, validatable       Tabular, schema          Natural language + unreliable documents
  Execution cost        CPU, nearly zero         CPU/GPU inference        Billed tokens or dedicated GPUs, P99 latency
  External dependency   Few                      Batch data               Third-party API, vector index, agent tools

::: note
[Module thread]{.tag} Each chapter contributes one building block of the same application: an enterprise assistant over internal documents (Confluence/SharePoint), with RAG, guardrails, and a budget. Lab 12 assembles it. The references "LLMs module ch. N" point to the M2 module *Large Language Models*; "Graph ML ch. 11" to the GraphRAG of the M1 module *Graph Machine and Deep Learning*.
:::

## 1. Lifecycle: versioning data, features, models {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a business RAG passes demos and fails in prod on 12% of queries (chunks too large, no golden set). This chapter fixes measurement loops.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Unversioned prompts; no regression eval; serving without token budgets / timeouts; confusing mean latency with p95.
:::

The ML lifecycle extends well beyond training: **collection → labeling → features → training → evaluation → registry → deployment → monitoring → (re)training**. Every arrow in this cycle is an artifact that must be *identified immutably*; failing that, no metric is reproducible — neither for debugging, nor for audits, nor in front of a client.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Artifact and lineage]{.tag} An **artifact** is any object produced or consumed by the cycle: dataset, feature schema, weights, tokenizer, prompt template, vector index, configuration, container image. The **lineage** is the graph of artifact → artifact dependencies. A training is *reproducible* when code + data + configuration + environment are all identified by fingerprints (hashes) and replayable.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — The triple fingerprint]{.tag} A training run is reproducible only if one can replay the triplet $(\text{code}, \text{data}, \text{config})$. In practice: `git` versions the code (commit hash), **DVC** versions the data and the weights (content fingerprint, the living file staying out of the repository), and `params.yaml` links the two. Every published metric references the three fingerprints — otherwise it is not a measurement, it is a rumor.
:::

```python
# Bulky data versioned by content (DVC) -- only the pointer goes into git
$ dvc add data/faq_2026.parquet          # creates data/faq_2026.parquet.dvc (hash + size)
$ git add data/faq_2026.parquet.dvc && git commit -m "faq v3 (dedup + PII scrub)"

# Declarative pipeline: stages re-run if and only if their inputs change
# dvc.yaml
stages:
  prepare:
    cmd: python src/prepare.py data/raw/ data/train.parquet
    deps: [data/raw/, src/prepare.py]
    outs: [data/train.parquet]
  finetune:
    cmd: python src/train_lora.py --config params.yaml
    deps: [data/train.parquet, src/train_lora.py, params.yaml]
    outs: [artifacts/lora_faq_v3/]
  evaluate:
    cmd: python src/evaluate.py --run artifacts/lora_faq_v3/
    deps: [artifacts/lora_faq_v3/, data/eval_v3.parquet]
    metrics: [artifacts/lora_faq_v3/metrics.json:
              {cache: false}]

$ dvc exp run            # replays the chain, records the experiment
$ dvc metrics diff       # compares v2 -> v3
```

### 1.1. Feature stores and registries

For tabular ML, a **feature store** (e.g. Feast) serves the same feature definition *offline* (training, batch) and *online* (serving, low-latency), eliminating training/inference skew — the sneakiest class of bug in industrial ML. For LLMs, the functional equivalent is twofold: the **prompt cache** (shared prefixes; cf. ch. 4) and the **embedding bank** of the RAG (ch. 6), whose schema (chunk type, embedding model, index version) must be managed like a feature: identified, versioned, replayable.

The **model registry** (MLflow, or a privatized `hf_hub` directory) records for each version: the fingerprints of the triplet, the qualification metrics, the signature (inputs/outputs), and the status (*staging / production / archived*). A deployment never references "the latest training" but a frozen version of the registry.

::: note
[LLM specificity: prompts and evals are artifacts]{.tag} In an LLM application, three families of artifacts add to the classic triplet: (i) **prompt templates** (versioned like code, with tests — ch. 2); (ii) **evaluation sets** (golden sets question → expected answer / relevant documents); (iii) the **embedding models and index** of the RAG, coupled: changing the embedding model invalidates the whole index (ch. 6). Forgetting to version a prompt is equivalent to not versioning the weights.
:::

  Step                    Artifact               Typical tool             Fingerprint
  ----------------------- ---------------------- ------------------------ ------------------------
  Data                    train/eval sets        DVC, lakeFS              content hash
  Features / embeddings   definitions, index     Feast, vector database   schema version
  Training                run + weights + LoRA   MLflow, HF Hub           run id + commit
  Evaluation              reports, metrics       MLflow, RAGAS            eval set hash
  Deployment              container image        OCI registry             sha256 digest
  Serving                 logs, traces           OTel, Langfuse           model + prompt + index

## 2. CI/CD for ML: testing data and models {#ch2}

The continuous integration of an ML system tests *four* layers, in order of increasing cost: the code, the data, the model, the infrastructure. The golden rule: make the pipeline fail **as early as possible**, at the cheapest level.

### 2.1. Data tests

Data is an interface like any other: one writes contracts for it. A **data contract** checks: the schema (types, columns, bounds), business invariants (allowed nulls, ranges), and statistical properties (duplication rate, distribution of a key column). Tools: Pandera (contracts in Python, executed in the pipeline), Great Expectations (declarative validation suites), quality servers integrated into platforms.

```python
import pandera as pa
import pandas as pd

schema = pa.DataFrameSchema({
    "question": pa.Column(str, pa.Check.str_length(3, 2000)),
    "answer":   pa.Column(str, pa.Check.str_length(1, 8000), nullable=True),
    "lang":     pa.Column(str, pa.Check.isin(["fr", "en"])),
    "doc_ids":  pa.Column(pa.List(str), pa.Check.list_length(1, 10)),
    "n_tokens": pa.Column(int, pa.Check.ge(0), pa.Check.le(4096)),
})

def validate(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return schema.validate(df, lazy=True)   # collects ALL errors
```

### 2.2. Model tests — and prompt tests

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Model non-regression test]{.tag} Let a fixed qualification set $D_{\text{qual}}$ and a metric $m$ (F1, accuracy rate, refusal rate, mean cost). The candidate $f_{\text{new}}$ replaces $f_{\text{prod}}$ if $m(f_{\text{new}}) \geq m(f_{\text{prod}}) - \tau$, where $\tau$ is the tolerance margin. The subtle point: $m$ is measured on a *sample* — deciding with a measured gap requires knowing when it is *significant*.
:::

::: thm
[Proposition 2.2 — Decision threshold by concentration (Hoeffding)]{.tag} Let $\ell$ be a loss bounded in $[0,1]$, measured on $n$ i.i.d. examples. With probability $\geq 1-\delta$ (on both sides): $$\bigl\|\;\mathbb{E}[\ell] - \widehat{\ell}_n\;\bigr\| \;\leq\; \sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.$$ To decide a rollback at $\delta = 0.05$ on $n = 1000$ examples, two models whose losses differ by less than $\sqrt{\log 40 / 2000} \approx 0.027$ are not *distinguishable*: the observed gap may be sampling noise.
:::

::: proof
The Hoeffding bound (proved in the ML module) applies to the $n$ i.i.d. variables $\ell_i \in [0,1]$: $\mathbb{P}\bigl(\|\overline{\ell} - \mathbb{E}\ell\| \geq t\bigr) \leq 2e^{-2nt^2}$. Setting the right-hand side to $\delta$ yields $t = \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}$. To compare two models one applies it to the variable $\ell_{\text{new}} - \ell_{\text{prod}}$ (bounded in $[-1,1]$, a factor 2 over the range — hence a factor 2 under the root). With $n=1000$, $\delta = 0.05$ and the signed version: $t \approx 2.8\,‰$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Practical consequence]{.tag} A "+0.4% F1" measured on 500 examples proves nothing: the 95% confidence interval is on the order of ±4 points for a metric at 50%. CI gateways must therefore require a *minimal* gap (margin $\tau$ *and* significance), under pain of "dancing on the noise" — a rollback here, a rollback there, and a slow drift of quality.
:::

Model tests also come in **slices**: performance per language, per context length, per topic, per user category — a global aggregate can mask a localized drop (a fairness theme, cf. Emerging ML module ch. 6). For an LLM, **prompt tests** add on: output format (valid JSON, schema), refusal guarantees (forbidden phrases), determinism wrappers (temperature 0, seed) and an **LLM judge** as oracle (ch. 5) — the judge itself being versioned and tested on a golden set.

```python
# .github/workflows/eval-gate.yml (excerpt) -- CPU gates first, GPU last
jobs:
  unit:                      # 1. code: fast tests, no model
    steps: [run: pytest tests/unit -x -q]
  data:                      # 2. data: pandera contracts on the day's delta
    steps: [run: python -m src.validate_delta --date $(date -d yesterday +%F)]
  eval:                      # 3. model: golden set + judge + prompt contracts
    steps:
      - run: python -m src.eval_llm --model staging --golden data/eval_v3.parquet
      - run: python -m src.gate --min-faithfulness 0.85 --max-regression 0.01
  deploy:                    # 4. progressive deployment (canary 5% -> 50% -> 100%)
    needs: [unit, data, eval]
    steps: [run: ./deploy.sh --canary 5]
```

### 2.3. Continuous delivery: canary and shadow

The deployment of an ML component is *progressive*: **shadow** (the new model receives duplicated traffic, its output is logged but not served — zero risk, double cost), **canary** (5% of traffic, automatic rollback if the guard metrics — latency, error rate, negative feedback — degrade), then full rollout. Rollback must be *a single button*: the previous version (weights + prompt + index) stays deployable in one command, thanks to the registry of ch. 1.

## 3. LLM serving: continuous batching, P99 latency {#ch3}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder — LLMs module ch. 6 (inference)
:::

Autoregressive decoding generates one token per forward pass; attention requires retaining the keys/values of all past tokens (KV cache); quantization reduces the weights and the KV; the per-token complexity grows with the context length. This chapter moves from "how it computes" to "how it holds a load".
::::

### 3.1. Batching: from one request to N

A GPU executes a decoding step in a time nearly *independent* of the number of sequences present in the batch (as long as memory and bandwidth allow): the operations are parallel and the GPU is *memory-bound* on the weights. Serving $B$ sequences simultaneously therefore divides the cost *per token* by almost $B$ — this is the economic argument for shared serving. Naive batching (*static batching*) waits to have $B$ requests, processes them as a block, and leaves the GPUs idle as soon as a short sequence finishes: yet a 20-token request ends quickly, and the batch becomes sparse.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Continuous batching (Orca, OSDI 2022)]{.tag} Schedule serving *at the iteration level* rather than the request level: at every decoding step, finished sequences leave the batch and waiting requests enter it. The GPU no longer idles between two requests. Combined with *selective batching* (batched operations where possible, per-request loops elsewhere), Orca claims up to 36.9× the throughput of prior systems at equal latency.
:::

```python
# Continuous batching loop (simplified) -- the heart of every modern LLM server
running, queue = [], deque()

def step():
    # 1) decoding: one iteration for ALL active sequences (a single GPU call)
    outputs = model.forward_batch([s.tokens for s in running])
    # 2) remove finished sequences (EOS or max length)
    for s in [s for s in running if s.finished(outputs)]:
        running.remove(s); s.finalize()
    # 3) admit new requests as long as the KV memory allows
    while queue and kv_pool.has_room(queue[0].prompt_len):
        running.append(queue.popleft().prefill())
    # 4) preemptive scheduling: if the KV saturates, evict (recompute/swap)
```

### 3.2. Memory: the KV cache and PagedAttention

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — KV cache size]{.tag} For a transformer with $L$ layers, $h\_{\\text{kv}}$ key/value heads (GQA) of dimension $d_h$, in precision $b$ bytes, the cache of a sequence of $T$ tokens occupies: $$M_{\text{KV}} \;=\; 2 \cdot L \cdot h_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_h \cdot b \cdot T \;\text{bytes}.$$ *Example* (Llama-3-8B: $L=32$, $h\_{\\text{kv}}=8$, $d_h=128$, fp16 $b=2$): $2\\times32\\times8\\times128\\times2 = 131,072$ bytes ≈ 128 KiB **per token**, i.e. 1 GiB for 8,192 tokens — more than some models weigh in significant bits.
:::

::: proof
Direct counting. Each layer $l$ stores, for each token $t$, a key $k_t\^{(l)}$ and a value $v_t\^{(l)}$, each a vector of $h\_{\\text{kv}} \\cdot d_h$ coefficients (the "query" attention heads may be more numerous — GQA — but only the K/V heads are cached). Each coefficient costs $b$ bytes: per layer and per token, $2\\,h\_{\\text{kv}}d_h b$ bytes; multiplying by $L$ layers and $T$ tokens gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Continuous batching therefore makes memory occupancy oscillate at every iteration (sequences entering/leaving). Allocating the KV as one maximal contiguous block (maximum output length reserved in advance) wastes: vLLM (SOSP 2023) treats the KV cache like the virtual memory of an OS — **pages** of 16 tokens, allocated on demand, non-contiguous, shareable between sequences derived from the same prefix (system prompt shared by thousands of requests): waste reduced to \~4% versus more than 60% for static allocation, throughput 2-4× prior systems. Ops consequence: the *real capacity* of a server is measured in "available KV tokens", not in concurrent requests.

### 3.3. Latency: TTFT, TPOT, P99

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — LLM serving SLO]{.tag} **TTFT** (time to first token): request → first token delay — dominated by the *prefill* (prompt) and the waiting queue. **TPOT** (time per output token): generation cadence — dominated by decoding and batch contention. **P99**: 99th percentile of a latency distribution — the relevant contractual commitment; the average masks queues. A typical interactive assistant SLO: TTFT P99 < 1.5 s, TPOT P99 < 80 ms/token.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Little's law]{.tag} In a stable system in steady state, with $L$ average clients present, $\\lambda$ clients arriving per second on average and $W$ mean sojourn time: $$L \;=\; \lambda\, W.$$ Serving corollary: at an imposed generation cadence ($W$ fixed by the number of tokens and the TPOT), the number of *concurrent* requests supported is $L = \\lambda W$ — the necessary concurrency grows linearly with the targeted throughput.
:::

::: proof
Proof by an output argument (direct). Over an interval $[0, t]$, let $A(t)$ be the number of arrivals and $D(t)$ the number of departures. The mean number of clients present is written $L_t = \\frac{1}{t}\\int_0\^t N(u)\\,du$, where $N(u)$ = present at instant $u$. Each request contributes to this integral exactly its sojourn time: $\\int_0\^t N(u)\\,du = \\sum\_{i \\,\\text{departed by} \\leq t} W_i + $ (residuals of requests still present). Dividing by $t$ and letting $t\\to\\infty$ (stability: $A(t)/t \\to \\lambda$, bounded residuals become negligible), one obtains $L = \\lambda\\, W$ — the argument requires no independence or distribution assumption; it is purely accounting. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Throughput versus latency: the batch trade-off]{.tag} Increasing $B$ (target batch) improves throughput (amortized cost/token) but lengthens the waiting queue — hence the TTFT P99. Modern servers expose this trade-off: *max_num_seqs*, token budgets per step, and preemption policies (recompute vs swap). Rule of thumb: size the target batch so that KV occupancy stays below \~90%, and let the autoscaler (ch. 3.4) absorb spikes rather than growing the batch beyond the SLO.
:::

### 3.4. Autoscaling

The relevant signal for scaling an LLM server is not CPU but: the **waiting queue length** (requests pending admission), the **mean waiting time** (TTFT − prefill time) and the **KV occupancy rate**. Horizontal autoscaling (HPA on a custom Prometheus metric) adds replicas; watch out for *warm-up spikes* (weight loading: tens of seconds to minutes — pre-pull the images, or pay the P99). For multi-GPU models (tensor parallel; cf. Emerging ML module ch. 2 on distributed computing), each replica is a *group* of GPUs; scaling changes the granularity of parallelism, not just the number of pods.

```python
# Launch a vLLM server exposing an (OpenAI-compatible) API on port 8000
$ docker run --gpus all -p 8000:8000 vllm/vllm-openai:v0.6 \
    --model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \
    --max-num-seqs 256 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
    --enable-prefix-caching            # reuse the KV of shared prefixes

# Async benchmark: TTFT / TPOT P50-P99 as a function of concurrency
import asyncio, time, statistics, httpx

async def one(client, prompt, n_out=256):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); first = None; n = 0
    async with client.stream("POST", "/v1/chat/completions",
            json={"model": "...", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                  "max_tokens": n_out, "stream": True}) as r:
        async for chunk in r.aiter_lines():
            if chunk.startswith("data:") and '"content"' in chunk:
                first = first or time.perf_counter() - t0   # TTFT
                n += 1
    return first, (time.perf_counter() - t0 - first) / n    # (TTFT, TPOT)

async def main(conc=64):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="http://localhost:8000",
                                 timeout=300) as c:
        res = await asyncio.gather(*[one(c, "Summarize this report in 5 points.")
                                     for _ in range(conc)])
    p = lambda x, q: sorted(x)[int(q * len(x))]
    ttft = [r[0] for r in res]; tpot = [r[1] for r in res]
    print(f"conc={conc}  TTFT p50/p99 = {p(ttft,.5):.2f}/{p(ttft,.99):.2f}s"
          f"  TPOT p99 = {p(tpot,.99)*1e3:.0f}ms")

for conc in (1, 4, 16, 64, 256): asyncio.run(main(conc))
```

  Metric                      Definition            Dominated by                 Typical target (chat)
  --------------------------- --------------------- ---------------------------- -----------------------
  TTFT P50 / P99              first token           prefill, queue               < 0.4 / < 1.5 s
  TPOT P99                    ms/token afterwards   decoding, contention         < 80 ms
  Throughput (tokens/s/GPU)   aggregated output     batch size, KV available     maximize under SLO
  KV occupancy                \% pages used         concurrency × length         < 90%
  Rejected requests           timeouts / 429        saturation, slow autoscale   \~0

## 4. Costs: euros per million tokens {#ch4}

Every LLM architecture decision sooner or later reduces to a cost per million tokens (Mt). APIs bill the *input* (prompt: amortizable by caching) and the *output* (generation: expensive) separately; the 2025-2026 orders of magnitude roughly span, from the small open-weight model to the frontier model, **from a few cents to a few tens of euros per Mt** — rates that change several times a year: any precise figure in course materials would be stale; the *method* of computation, on the other hand, remains.

::: prop
[Proposition 4.1 — Unit cost of self-hosted serving]{.tag} If a server delivers a sustained throughput of $R$ tokens/s (outputs, continuous batching) on GPUs costing $c$ €/h (rental all inclusive), the operational cost per million output tokens equals: $$\text{cost/Mt} \;=\; \frac{c}{R} \cdot \frac{10^6}{3600} \;\approx\; 278 \cdot \frac{c}{R} \;\; \text{€/Mt}.$$ *Example*: an 8B on a GPU at \~2 €/h delivering $R = 2,000$ tokens/s in batch → ≈ 0.28 €/Mt; the same GPU on isolated requests (batch 1, $R \approx 60$) → ≈ 9 €/Mt. **Batching is a factor of 30 on the bill.**
:::

::: proof
The server produces $R$ tokens per second; each billed hour at $c$ € therefore produces $3600\,R$ tokens; the cost per token is $c/(3600\,R)$ €, and per million tokens $10^6 c/(3600 R) = 277.8\, c/R$. The direct division by $R$: doubling the throughput halves the cost per token at constant hardware — this is the economic justification of ch. 3. [∎]{.qed}
:::

### 4.1. The saving levers

-   **Prefix cache**: shared system prompt + history → the prefill is billed/consumed once; on the API side, *prompt caching* reduces the input cost of repeated prefixes (often billed at a discount); on the vLLM side, the KV is reused for free.
-   **Model routing (cascade)**: small model first, escalation to the big one if the small one "is not sure" (confidence score, agreement of two candidates, or a classifier). The sequential decision formalized as a bandit (cf. RL module ch. 6): one arbitrates cost vs quality request by request.
-   **Output limit**: output costs \~5-10× the input; constraining `max_tokens` and the format (answer in k points, short JSON) is the most underrated lever.
-   **Quantization** (cf. LLMs ch. 6; Advanced Topics ch. 6): 4 bits ≈ ×2-3 in throughput on the weights — and smaller GPUs.
-   **Deferred batch processing**: non-interactive tasks (archive classification) go in nightly batches; some APIs bill these modes \~50% cheaper.

  Criterion              Managed API                                           Self-hosted (open weights)
  ---------------------- ----------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------
  Low-usage cost         Pay-per-token, optimal                                Brutal GPU amortization
  High-usage cost        Linear, becomes expensive                             \~0.1-1 €/Mt depending on batch (prop. 4.1)
  Sensitive data         Contract, jurisdiction, zero-retention to negotiate   Total control (closed network)
  P99 latency            The provider's                                        Controllable (ch. 3), at your own expense
  Ability to fine-tune   Limited (hosted LoRAs depending on the offering)      Total (ch. 7)
  Ops                    Nearly zero                                           Team + on-call + GPU supply

::: note
[Multilingual and real costs]{.tag} The per-token bill interacts with tokenization (cf. LLMs module ch. 1): a French corpus typically costs 15-25% more tokens than an equivalent English corpus with the dominant tokenizers. The "price per word" therefore depends on the language — an argument for measuring (exercise 5) rather than trusting round conversion tables.
:::

## 5. Evaluation in production: drift and monitoring {#ch5}

### 5.1. Data drift, concept drift

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Drift]{.tag} **Data drift**: the distribution of inputs changes ($P(X)$ moves — new topics, new user population, new documentary source). **Concept drift**: the input → correct answer relation changes ($P(Y\mid X)$ moves — yesterday's "good" answer becomes wrong: regulation, company merger, vocabulary). For a RAG, a third drift: the **corpus** changes (ch. 6).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — PSI = Jeffreys divergence]{.tag} The population stability index (PSI), summed over the bins $i$ of a histogram: $$\mathrm{PSI}(p, q) \;=\; \sum_i \bigl(p_i - q_i\bigr)\, \ln\frac{p_i}{q_i} \;=\; \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) + \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p),$$ is exactly the Jeffreys divergence: symmetric, zero iff $p = q$. Usual thresholds in credit risk: PSI < 0.1 stable; 0.1-0.25 to watch; > 0.25 alert.
:::

::: proof
Let us expand: $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = \sum_i p_i \ln(p_i/q_i)$ and $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \sum_i q_i \ln(q_i/p_i)$. The sum equals $\sum_i (p_i - q_i)\ln(p_i/q_i)$ — precisely the PSI. Each term is positive (the two factors $p_i - q_i$ and $\ln(p_i/q_i)$ have the same sign); zero if and only if $p_i = q_i$ for all $i$. Symmetry is obvious from the summed form. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The classic detectors: PSI/KL per feature (interpretable, bin by bin), Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (comparison of continuous distributions, cf. Refresher Statistics), MMD distance (ML module), and stream detectors (ADWIN) for online signals. For an LLM, the "features" to monitor are: prompt length, language, topics (lightweight classifier), presence of injected documents, truncation rate — *and* output proxies: refusal rate, "I don't know" rate, median answer length, JSON parse failure rate. Without online labels, one monitors *symptoms*; the true metrics come from feedback and sampling.

### 5.2. Monitoring: three time loops

  Loop        Latency         Signals                                                           Action
  ----------- --------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------
  Reactive    second-minute   latency, 5xx errors, 429, KV saturation, cost/req                 autoscale, throttle, rollback
  Daily       day             PSI per feature, refusal rate, feedback 👎, sampled RAGAS eval    ticket, investigation, prompt fix
  Strategic   week-month      concept drift (refreshed golden set eval), cost drift, adoption   retraining/fine-tune, model migration

The metrics of an LLM application stack up: infra (GPU, memory); serving (ch. 3); **quality** (explicit feedback, sampled evals); **safety** (guardrail trigger rate, injection attempts — cf. ch. 8 and the Explainability/Security module). The structural watchpoint: the **feedback loop** — the data collected in production (real questions, feedback) become tomorrow's training data: the model steers the distribution it will later see (selection bias, rich-get-richer). Documenting this loop is part of the audit (ch. 9; Emerging ML module ch. 6 on fairness).

### 5.3. The LLM judge in CI and production

::: note
[Judge: how, and with which biases]{.tag} A judge model evaluates (question, answer) pairs against a rubric (fidelity to context, completeness, tone); Zheng et al. (MT-Bench, NeurIPS 2023) show agreement with humans > 80% on conversation tasks — *but* with documented biases: preference for the first position, for long answers, and *self-preference* (the judge favors its own style). Good practices: alternated order, explicit rubric, reference provided, human golden set to calibrate the judge, judge version frozen in CI (ch. 1). The judge is a *noisy sensor* — one uses it to detect regressions, not to certify.
:::

```python
# Mini regression judge in CI: compares prod vs candidate on the golden set
def judge_pair(question, ref, ans_prod, ans_cand, judge):
    rub = "Expected answer (reference): {ref}\nA: {a}\nB: {b}\n" \
          "Which one is more faithful to the reference? Answer A, B, or EQUAL."
    out = judge(f"Q: {question}\n" + rub.format(ref=ref, a=ans_prod, b=ans_cand))
    out_sw = judge(f"Q: {question}\n" + rub.format(ref=ref, a=ans_cand, b=ans_prod))
    pair = {out.strip()[:4], out_sw.strip()[:4]}      # alternated order, anti-bias
    return "cand" if pair == {"A", "B"} else ("prod" if pair == {"B", "A"} else "equal")

# gate: no significant regression (cf. prop. 2.2 for the minimal margin)
wins = sum(judge_pair(**ex) == "cand" for ex in golden)
assert wins >= 0.45 * len(golden), f"judge regression: {wins}/{len(golden)}"
```

## 6. RAG Ops: freshness and continuous evaluation {#ch6}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder — LLMs module ch. 7 (RAG)
:::

Pipeline: chunking → embeddings → vector index → retrieval (hybrid BM25 + dense, cf. NLP ch. 2 and 7) → reranking → conditioned generation. This chapter treats that pipeline as a *data system* with freshness and evaluation contracts — not as a demo.
::::

### 6.1. Incremental indexing and freshness

The enterprise corpus moves: Confluence pages edited, contracts signed, FAQs enriched. The index must follow with an explicit **freshness SLA** ("a published document is queryable within 15 minutes"). The standard pattern: *change data capture* (webhooks/API of the document repository) → event queue → incremental *upsert* into the index, key = (source, doc_id, version). Subtleties:

-   **Idempotence**: replaying the same event twice must create only one batch of vectors; deduplicate by key, mark obsolete chunks (soft delete) so as not to break the evaluation links;
-   **Per-document atomicity**: the chunks of a document v2 replace those of v1 *as a block* (otherwise retrieval mixes the versions);
-   **Embeddings ↔ index coupling**: changing the embedding model requires *re-embedding* the whole corpus (the spaces are mutually incompatible); dual-boot of the index during the migration, then switchover — the index is a versioned artifact in the sense of ch. 1;
-   **Freshness ≠ total reindexing**: measure the cost (summary tokens, GPU time) and aim for incremental everywhere possible.

### 6.2. Evaluating a RAG without humans: RAGAS

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — RAGAS metrics (Es et al., 2023)]{.tag} Four *reference-free* metrics, computed by LLM decomposition: **faithfulness** (is every claim of the answer attested by the context? — anti-hallucination), **answer relevancy** (does the answer answer the question?), **context precision** (are the relevant chunks indeed ranked first?) and **context recall** (are the necessary chunks retrieved? — requires a reference answer). The last two isolate the *retrieval*, the first two the *generation*: this is the diagnostic grid missing from a global F1.
:::

```python
from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import (faithfulness, answer_relevancy,
                           context_precision, context_recall)
from datasets import Dataset

ds = Dataset.from_dict({
    "question":     q_list,          # golden set (ch. 1: version this set!)
    "answer":       answers,         # outputs of the candidate pipeline
    "contexts":     retrieved_chunks,
    "ground_truth": ref_answers,     # for context_recall
})
report = evaluate(ds, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy,
                               context_precision, context_recall])
# CI gate: faithfulness >= 0.85; weekly panel: the 4 time series
```

::: note
[Reading a RAGAS report like an engineer]{.tag} *Low recall, high faithfulness*: retrieval is failing — improve chunking, hybrid, reranker. *High recall, low faithfulness*: the model invents despite the context — prompt, stronger model, forced citation. *Low relevancy*: off-topic or verbose answer. The trap of *reference-free* metrics: their judge has the biases of ch. 5 — one calibrates them on a hand-annotated sample before making them CI thresholds.
:::

### 6.3. The graph to the rescue of RAG

Vector RAG fails on *global* questions ("what are the recurring themes of the 2025 reports?") that require aggregating the whole corpus; GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024; cf. Graph ML module ch. 11) builds an entity graph (LLM extraction), partitions it into communities (Leiden) and summarizes each community — the global answer becomes a *map-reduce* over the summaries. The ops cost: LLM indexing is expensive (every document goes through extraction calls), hence *incremental by necessity*; communities are recomputed periodically. The arbitration (vector vs graph vs hybrid) belongs in the system's ablation table — and must be re-measured at every model migration (ch. 2).

## 7. Fine-tuning Ops: versioned LoRAs {#ch7}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder — LLMs module ch. 4-5: SFT, LoRA, DPO
:::

Instruction fine-tuning (SFT) adapts the model; LoRA (Hu et al., ICLR 2022) freezes the weights $W$ and learns only $\Delta W = BA$ of rank $r \ll d$: a few tens of MB instead of GB, trainable on a single GPU. DPO/RLHF (ch. 5) then align the preferences.
::::

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Versioned adapter]{.tag} An *adapter* (LoRA) is usable only when coupled with: (i) its **exact base** (name + version of the weights); (ii) its **prompt template**; (iii) its **training data** (hash); (iv) its **hyperparameters** ($r$, $\alpha$, target modules). The unit of versioning is not the `.safetensors` file but this quintuple — a LoRA on the "wrong" base (same architecture, different checkpoint) produces silently degraded outputs.
:::

```python
# Adapter registry: the record is the authority (MLflow / private HF Hub / simple CSV)
adapter:        faq-v3-lora
base:           meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct@9c6b4c1d   # exact hash
template:       prompts/faq_chat_v2.jinja                      # git version
data:           data/faq_2026.parquet @ sha256=4f2a...         # DVC
lora_config:    {r: 16, alpha: 32, target: [q_proj, v_proj]}
metrics:        {eval_v3_f1: 0.91, faithfulness: 0.88, judge_winrate: 0.56}
trained_by:     pipeline#2026-03-11, run_id 7c3e...
deployed:       canary 5% since 2026-03-13, SLO OK
```

### 7.1. The fine-tuning cycle in production

1.  **Collect**: feedback 👍/👎, expert corrections, questions without a good answer (failed queries from monitoring — ch. 5);
2.  **Clean / deduplicate / anonymize**: deduplication reduces memorization (cf. Explainability/Security module ch. 7);
3.  **Build the pairs** (SFT) then preferences (DPO) — balance of domains, slices evaluated separately (ch. 2);
4.  **Train** LoRA on the *frozen* base; log the quintuple;
5.  **Qualify**: golden set + judge + safety tests (fine-tuning can *degrade* refusals!) — gate of ch. 2;
6.  **Deploy in canary** with rollback (ch. 2.3);
7.  **Measure the impact** (winrate, cost, latency) before generalization — fine-tuning must win against simply improving the prompt *and* against RAG, otherwise it has no reason to exist.

::: note
[Multi-LoRA serving]{.tag} Use case: a single 8B engine serves ten clients, each with its own LoRA (tone, domain, language). Modern servers load several adapters on a base shared in memory — a single copy of the weights, the $\Delta W$ (a few tens of MB) being applied per request. The ops work consists of guaranteeing the routing (client header → adapter) and the isolation of evaluations per tenant (slices of ch. 2). The base rarely changes; the adapters often: two distinct deployment cadences in the same pipeline.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Size of a LoRA]{.tag} A rank-$r$ LoRA on a layer $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$ stores $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}$, i.e. $r\,(d_{\text{out}} + d_{\text{in}})$ parameters instead of $d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}}$. On the attention projections of an 8B ($d = 4096$, ≈ 7 targeted layers of the q/v type out of 32, $r = 16$): \~0.1% of the parameters — a few tens of MB in fp16. The storage saving is a bonus; the decisive saving is the *training cost* (no optimizer state on the frozen weights) and the *deployment cadence* (adapter hot-swap).
:::

## 8. Agents in production: tracing and guardrails {#ch8}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminder — LLMs module ch. 8 (agents)
:::

An agent = an LLM in a loop (observation → reasoning → action via tools), with memory and possibly multi-step planning. This chapter adds no intelligence: it adds *observability*, the *budgets* and the *permissions* without which an agent is undebuggable and dangerous.
::::

### 8.1. Tracing: the tree of calls

An agent request unfolds in dozens of nested LLM and tool calls. The central datum is the **trace**: a tree of *spans* (one span per call: input, output, token cost, latency, model, attempt), OpenTelemetry-compliant — the vendors Langfuse/W&B Weave plug into it. Without a trace: no ability to answer "why did the agent send this email?". With a trace: deterministic replay (by logging the seeds/times), bottleneck analysis (which tool dominates the latency?), per-step costs, and detection of behavioral anomalies (loops: same tool, same arguments, N times).

```python
// OTel span of an agent call (excerpt) -- everything is there for replay and cost
{
  "trace_id": "a1b2...", "span_id": "17", "parent_id": "03",
  "name": "llm.call",
  "attributes": {
    "llm.model": "llama3-8b-instruct@v3-lora-faq",
    "llm.prompt_hash": "9e21...",         // -> versioned template (ch. 1)
    "llm.input_tokens": 1842, "llm.output_tokens": 96,
    "llm.cost_eur": 0.00042, "llm.latency_ms": 741,
    "agent.step": 4, "agent.tool": "search_confluence",
    "rag.index_version": "2026-03-11.2"
  }
}
```

### 8.2. Guardrails: in layers, around the loop

  Layer         Mechanism                                  Example
  ------------- ------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------
  Input         validation, injection classifiers, quota   block 500 kB prompts, injection detector (Security module ch. 5-6)
  Loop          maximum budgets                            max 15 steps, max 0.10 €/task, global timeout
  Action        per-tool permissions, scoping              read-only on Confluence; sending e-mails = human confirmation
  Output        format and content validators              strict JSON schema; no bank details in the answers
  Execution     sandbox (ch. 9)                            code run in an ephemeral container with no outbound network
  Observation   behavioral alerts                          loop rate, success per task, cost drift

::: ex
[Example 8.1 — The budget as the first guardrail]{.tag} A monitoring agent performs on average 6 LLM calls + 3 tool calls per task. A malicious user (or a booby-trapped document — indirect injection, cf. Security module ch. 5) can make it loop: each iteration re-injects a bit of context. Cap *per task*: steps ≤ 15, tokens ≤ 50 k, cost ≤ 0.10 € — and cut off cleanly (degraded answer: "I could not finish"): the failure becomes a *bounded cost* instead of a billing incident.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — Per-task success collapses with length]{.tag} If each step succeeds independently with probability $p$, a task of $k$ steps succeeds with $p^k$: $p = 0.95$ and $k = 20$ give 36%. Hence: (i) shorten the chains (more reliable tools, shallower plans); (ii) local retries and reflexivity; (iii) evaluate agents *per complete task*, never per step.
:::

### 8.3. Evaluating an agent

Agent metrics: **success rate per task** (on scripted tasks with an initial state and a success criterion — e.g. "the ticket is created with the right fields"), **average cost per task** (tokens × price + tools), **end-to-end P95 latency**, **human intervention rate**. The evaluation environments must be *replayable*: simulated tools (mock Confluence, mock mail) for CI, a sampled real environment for production — the simulation runs hundreds of tasks for a few cents.

## 9. Operational security: secrets, sandbox, supply chain {#ch9}

::: note
[Scope]{.tag} The attacks *against the model* (jailbreaks, injections, poisoning, extraction) are the subject of the M2 module *Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs*. Here: the security of the *system around* the model — the ops of an LLM application; the reference checklist of the field is the [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/).
:::

### 9.1. Secrets and identities

-   API keys, database passwords, index tokens: never in the code nor the images — a vault (Vault, Secret Manager) injected at startup; periodic rotation; repository scanners in CI (a secret committed = compromised, even "just on a branch");
-   Each service has **its** identity (service account) and **least privilege**: the RAG engine does not need write access to the corpus; the agent does not need the credentials of the administrative database;
-   The outputs of the LLM are *data*, never *instructions*: a model's response must never be evaluated/executed (eval, shell, SQL) without validation — the flaw class "the model generated the code, we execute it" is a special case of indirect injection (Security module ch. 5).

### 9.2. Sandbox and isolation

When the agent executes code (notebooks, "calculator" tools, plugins), execution must be **confined**: an ephemeral container, a temporary file system, outbound network blocked by default, CPU/RAM limits, a hardened runtime (e.g. gVisor/Firecracker for kernel-level isolation), and filtering of *exfiltrations* — including over slow channels (DNS queries, timing): an agent compromised by injection will try to exfiltrate via the only channel it was left (the tools! the mail! the displayed output?). Hence the duo permissions (ch. 8) + sandbox: the same principle as in system security — compromise is likely, **blast radius minimal**.

### 9.3. Supply chain

-   **Model weights**: downloaded from verified sources, sha256 fingerprint recorded in the registry (ch. 1) — an open-weight model is a dependency like a library, with "logical" CVEs (backdoors; cf. Security module ch. 5) and no automatic scanner;
-   **Dependencies**: lockfiles, SBOM, classic vulnerability scans in CI (same as any app);
-   **Prompts and adapters**: mandatory review — a prompt is code in disguise; a LoRA trained on unvalidated data is an opaque dependency;
-   **Logs**: the traces contain user text (personal data?) — limited retention, anonymization, controlled access; cf. Security module ch. 8-10 and the AI Act (ch. 10).

  Ops threat                    Vector               Countermeasure
  ----------------------------- -------------------- -----------------------------------------------
  API key theft                 repo, image, logs    vault + rotation + provider quotas
  Exfiltration by the agent     tool, mail, code     scoped permissions, egress deny, sandbox
  Payment denial (bill shock)   agent loop, spam     budgets (ch. 8), per-client quotas
  Booby-trapped model           backdoored weights   provenance + hash + safety evals (ch. 2)
  Leak via logs                 verbose traces       PII scrubbing, short retention, logged access

## 10. Case study and green ops {#ch10}

### 10.1. The stack of an enterprise assistant

Let us assemble the bricks. Specifications: 2,000 employees, SSO, Confluence + SharePoint corpus (\~500 kB documents), questions in French, sourced answers, no data outside the perimeter, annual budget of the order of a few tens of k€ of inference.

  Component        Typical choice                                    Chapter       Points of attention
  ---------------- ------------------------------------------------- ------------- -------------------------------------------
  Auth & gateway   SSO OIDC, per-user quotas                         ch. 9         identity = the key to agent permissions
  ingestion        CDC Confluence → chunks → embeddings              ch. 6         idempotence, 15 min freshness SLA
  Index            vector + BM25 (hybrid)                            ch. 6         versioned, dual-boot during migration
  Reranker         light cross-encoder                               ch. 6         +30 ms, −20% of context errors typically
  Generation       front model API *or* self-hosted 8B               ch. 3-4       routing according to document sensitivity
  Adaptation       LoRA "internal tone"                              ch. 7         rollback = adapter swap
  Agents           search + writing, read permissions                ch. 8         budgets, tracing, sandbox
  Evaluation       golden set of 500 Q/A + weekly RAGAS + CI judge   ch. 2, 5, 6   versioned set, slices by business line
  Monitoring       Prometheus + OTel + alerting                      ch. 3, 5, 8   P99 TTFT, PSI, cost/req, refusal rate

::: note
[Why not GraphRAG?]{.tag} If the dominant usage becomes "which teams work on topic X?" (*relational* questions), the entity graph (Graph ML module ch. 11; GraphRAG of Edge et al.) becomes profitable despite its indexing cost: the answer to the question "do we need a graph?" is a *measured trade-off* (RAGAS eval + ablation), not a fad.
:::

### 10.2. Green ops: measuring energy

The energy cost of LLMs concentrates (i) in **pre-training** — Patterson et al. (2021) formalize the carbon accounting of large trainings (consumption, regional electricity mix, PUE); Luccioni et al. (2022) do the same for BLOOM including the amortization of training; (ii) in aggregated **inference** — billions of requests of a few Wh each. For a *developer*, the useful unit is the consumption per request: measurable with CodeCarbon (CPU/GPU/PUE meter) around each serving point.

```python
from codecarbon import EmissionsTracker

with EmissionsTracker(measure_power_secs=1, log_level="warning") as tracker:
    answer = rag_pipeline.answer(question)      # full request

print(f"{tracker.total_energy_kWh * 1000:.1f} Wh for this request",
      f"({tracker.total_emissions * 1e3:.1f} gCO2e on the local mix)")
```

::: prop
[Proposition 10.1 — The four green levers, in order of effectiveness]{.tag} (1) **Functional sobriety**: routing to small models, shorter outputs, cache (ch. 4) — divides the energy without touching the hardware; (2) **Quantization**: \~2-4× on the energy throughput per token (cf. LLMs ch. 6); (3) **Batching**: the same GPU delivers more tokens/Wh in batch (ch. 3 — the two propositions 4.1 and 10.1 are the same equation, in euros and in Wh); (4) **Geographic and temporal scheduling**: moving the nightly batches to the low-carbon-mix regions at the right moment. The order matters: one does not buy green GPUs before having shortened the outputs.
:::

::: note
[LLGA position]{.tag} This module is deliberately transversal to the heart of the master: serving (ch. 3) extends the LLMs module, graph RAG (ch. 6) extends the Graph ML module, agents (ch. 8) extend the RL module, and evaluation in production (ch. 5) prepares the safety track of the Explainability, Security, Privacy module. The instructors of this proposed course are not yet confirmed: the cited standards and tools are authoritative; the LLGA (LLMs & Graphs) group of the X is mobilized when relevant.
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **Reproducibility (ch. 1).** Build a mini DVC pipeline (prepare → embed → eval) over 100 documents; modify a single document and predict which stages re-execute; verify. Show that a metric without the three fingerprints is not replayable.
2.  **Data contracts (ch. 2).** Write a Pandera schema for a FAQ set (question/answer/language/tokens) and make CI fail on: exact duplicate, empty answer, unknown language, abnormal length. Add the error report as an artifact.
3.  **Significance of a gate (ch. 2).** Simulate two models with losses 0.30 and 0.31 on n = 500; how many times does the "no regression" test wrongly fail over 100 draws? Deduce from it a realistic minimal margin for your CI.
4.  **Serving (ch. 3).** Deploy an 8B on vLLM; plot the TTFT P50/P99 and TPOT P99 curves for concurrency 1 → 256; locate the breaking point (KV occupancy); compare static batching (vary it) and continuous batching.
5.  **Little's law in practice (ch. 3).** From the traces of lab 4, estimate $\lambda$, $W$ and $L$ over a 10 min window; verify $L = \lambda W$ within ±10%; explain the gap (non-stationarity, preemption).
6.  **Accounting (ch. 4).** For a given workload (short questions, 300-token answers, 10 k req/day), quantify: API (input × in price, output × out price, prefix cache), self-hosted (proposition 4.1 with R measured in lab 4). Identify the crossover point in requests/day and its sensitivity to the utilization rate.
7.  **Drift (ch. 5).** Generate two weeks of simulated "logs" with a topic drift on day 9; implement PSI (prop. 5.2) and KS over the lengths and topics; tune the threshold for ≤ 1 false alert per week; document the detection delay / false alerts trade-off.
8.  **RAG Ops (ch. 6).** Take the RAG of the LLMs module ch. 7: move to incremental indexing (adding 20 documents at D+1 without full re-indexing); measure RAGAS before/after; trigger an embedding migration and run the index dual-boot.
9.  **Versioned LoRAs (ch. 7).** Train two LoRAs (r = 8, 32) on the same set; record the quintuples; serve both in multi-LoRA; evaluate; deliberately "forget" the base version and observe the silent degradation — then add the compatibility check to the registry.
10. **Observable agent (ch. 8).** Instrument a search + writing agent with OTel spans; inject three failures (a tool that times out, a retry loop, a too-long context); diagnose each one *only* through the traces; add budgets and caps, replay.
11. **Ops audit (ch. 9).** Put a mini LLM application through the sieve of the OWASP Top 10 LLM: list the findings, severity, fixes; check in particular: secrets, tool permissions, output validation, log retention.
12. **Common-thread lab (ch. 10).** Assemble the assistant: hybrid RAG + reranker + LoRA + guardrails + dashboard (latency, PSI, RAGAS, cost/req, Wh/req via CodeCarbon); present a "simulated post-mortem": a faithfulness regression is injected, the team must detect it (dashboard?) and roll back (registry) in less than 15 minutes.
